facts.text: We discussed using AAC audio with an appropriate bit rate for compatibility with HLS.
We discussed whether ffmpeg can transform AAC into an HLS compatible one.
We discussed why AAC is good at low bitrate.
We discussed why not use MP3 instead of AAC.
We discussed why MP3 is more popular and used than AAC in consumer music devices and apps.
We discussed an app that gets an AS67 audio stream and reads SCTE-104 ad data from a UDP ancillary payload.
We discussed that the app stitches audio ads to the AS67 audio stream and delivers the result in HLS to the end user.
We discussed whether the app should have PTP standard in place for this workflow.
We discussed that if the app just stitches audio ads to the stream and delivers it as an HLS stream, PTP implementation might be overkill.
We discussed SMPTE timecode usage in this context.
We discussed that the feed is an AES67 audio radio broadcast.
We discussed that for ad stitching in the app, the stream is expected to signal ad breaks via SCTE-104 implementation.
We discussed that SCTE-104 may be added to UDP packets.
We asked whether something is wrong with the described approach.
We asked whether ffmpeg can convert AAC to an HLS compatible format.
We discussed creating a HLS stream that references audio files in .aac.
We discussed internet radio broadcast and AES67-compatible ones.
We asked whether AAC is the de facto standard for internet radio broadcast and AES67-compatible ones.
We asked whether AAC is the most common thought.
